samples.text:
The bar chart shows how much carbon dioxide each person produced in eight countries in 1990 and 2020.

In 1990, USA had the highest emissions with 19.4 tonnes per person, and Australia was second with 16.2 tonnes. Germany and UK were 12.8 and 10.0 tonnes. The other four countries were much lower. China was 2.0 tonnes, Brazil 1.5, Nigeria 0.9 and India only 0.7 tonnes.

In 2020, the emissions in the first four countries goes down. The USA fell to 14.2 tonnes and Australia fell slightly to 15.0, so Australia became the highest. Germany decreased to 7.7 tonnes and UK decreased to 4.9, which is about half. However, China increase very much from 2.0 to 7.6 tonnes, it is almost the same like Germany. Brazil and India also rose a little to 2.1 and 1.7 tonnes. Only Nigeria went down to 0.6 tonnes.

Overall, the emissions per person fell in USA, Australia, Germany, UK and Nigeria, but it rose in China, Brazil and India.
samples.why: Accurate figures and a basic overview at the end · information listed rather than grouped · mechanical linking · limited range of vocabulary · article, agreement and tense errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
The chart compares carbon dioxide emissions per person in eight countries in 1990 and 2020.

Overall, the four countries with the highest emissions in 1990, namely the USA, Australia, Germany and the UK, all reduced their per capita figures over the period, while emissions rose in China, Brazil and India. Despite these changes, the USA and Australia remained the largest emitters.

In 1990, an average American produced 19.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide, the highest figure on the chart, followed by an average Australian at 16.2 tonnes. By 2020, the US figure had dropped considerably to 14.2 tonnes, while Australia's fell only slightly to 15.0 tonnes, making it the top emitter. Germany and the UK recorded even sharper decreases, from 12.8 to 7.7 tonnes and from 10.0 to 4.9 tonnes respectively, meaning the UK's emissions more or less halved.

The opposite trend can be seen in China, where emissions per person rose from just 2.0 tonnes to 7.6 tonnes, almost equal to Germany's level. Brazil and India also saw increase, to 2.1 and 1.7 tonnes, although their emissions remained low. Nigeria was the exception among the lower emitters, with its figure falling from 0.9 to 0.6 tonnes.
samples.why: Clear overview of opposing trends · key features highlighted with apt comparisons · well-organised paragraphs and varied linking · some less common vocabulary · one minor article slip.

samples.text:
The bar chart compares per capita carbon dioxide emissions in eight countries in 1990 and 2020.

The chart reveals a clear divergence between two groups of countries. The four highest emitters of 1990, the USA, Australia, Germany and the UK, all cut their emissions per person over the thirty years, whereas China, Brazil and India recorded increases. China's growth was by far the most dramatic.

In 1990, emissions were highest in the USA, at 19.4 tonnes per person, and Australia, at 16.2 tonnes. Although both figures had fallen by 2020, the reduction was far greater in the USA (to 14.2 tonnes) than in Australia (to 15.0 tonnes), so Australia ended the period with the highest per capita output. Germany and the UK achieved the steepest cuts: Germany's figure fell from 12.8 to 7.7 tonnes, and the UK's roughly halved, from 10.0 to 4.9 tonnes.

China, by contrast, saw its emissions per person almost quadruple, rising from 2.0 to 7.6 tonnes and very nearly drawing level with Germany. Increases in Brazil (1.5 to 2.1 tonnes) and India (0.7 to 1.7 tonnes) were much smaller in absolute terms, and Nigeria's figure actually fell slightly, from 0.9 to 0.6 tonnes, the lowest on the chart in 2020.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected around a clear divergence · well-placed overview · precise figures and derived comparisons · cohesion seamless · wide, accurate vocabulary · complex structures used flexibly and without error.
